Classification guard: the single authored edge asserts association only (etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, hypothesizedOnly:true). It records that dizziness is among the symptoms reported in the inappropriate-sinus-tachycardia syndrome in review-level descriptions of condition-specific series and cohorts, not that the tachycardia caused dizziness in any individual; the mechanism of the syndrome is described as multifactorial with autonomic dysfunction as the central abnormality, and an individual claim therefore requires documented heart-rate and rhythm data with chronology, symptom characterization, and exclusion of the competing causes of dizziness listed on the edge.

Duplicate-scope guard: the dizziness identity receives no prior incoming window, so this batch opens the first condition-specific window on that target; no cardiac-arrhythmia edge is authored because inappropriate sinus tachycardia is itself an arrhythmia and the edge would restate the identity (constitutive/umbrella guard), and no cardiomyopathy or congestive-heart-failure edge is authored because the largest condition-specific cohort found no cardiomyopathy and stable left ventricular ejection fraction over follow-up (negative-cohort guard).

Tachycardia-definition guard: the catalogue carries distinct postural-orthostatic-tachycardia-syndrome and vasovagal-syncope identities, and no edge is authored to either because inappropriate sinus tachycardia is defined by a resting sinus rate above the normal range in the absence of a primary cause, so the postural and reflex mechanisms belong to those identities' own primaries (parallel-pathway and direction-inversion guards).
governanceNotes: D1 batch 48 (2026-09-24): one bounded association edge authored - inappropriate sinus tachycardia to dizziness (rank 1), ASSOCIATION_ONLY with etiologicalConsensus NOT_ESTABLISHED, vaNexusProbabilityAlignment NOT_ASSERTED, hypothesizedOnly:true, and mechanismCategory MULTIFACTORIAL (autonomic dysregulation with heart-rate elevation rather than a single identified pathway). The proposition rests on the Ahmed 2022 JACC review topic of the week, which describes inappropriate sinus tachycardia as a clinical syndrome that generally affects young patients and is associated with distressing symptoms, states that the most common symptom is palpitations but that it can be accompanied by a myriad of symptoms including anxiety, dizziness, presyncope, and syncope, and records that the pathogenesis is not well understood and considered multifactorial with autonomic dysfunction as the central abnormality and that the diagnosis is one of exclusion, and on the Ruzieh 2018 review, which defines the syndrome as a resting sinus rate inexplicably above one hundred beats per minute associated with symptoms such as palpitations, dyspnoea, or dizziness in the absence of primary causes of tachycardia and lists the alternative causes that the diagnosis requires excluding (medications and substances, panic attacks, pulmonary embolism, fever, hyperthyroidism, hypovolaemia, anaemia, and pain). The edge is not raised to causation: the located evidence is review-level symptom enumeration rather than a condition-specific cohort measuring incident dizziness, the symptom complex overlaps the syndrome definition and includes anxiety, and dizziness in these patients may arise from the shared autonomic abnormality or from competing conditions rather than from the heart rate itself.

Negative-cohort screen recorded 2026-09-24: the Shabtaie 2020 Mayo Clinic review of 305 patients with inappropriate sinus tachycardia over a twenty-year period (mean follow-up 3.5 years, 92.1% female, mean age 33.2 years) reports a mean left ventricular ejection fraction of 62.3% at diagnosis with no significant change over a mean 4.9-year echocardiographic follow-up (59.8% versus 61.4%, p=0.2971) and concludes that there was no evidence of cardiomyopathy or mortality related to the condition, so no cardiomyopathy or congestive-heart-failure edge is authored despite case reports of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy; the cohort also records depression in 25.6% and anxiety in 24.6% as comorbid conditions without a psychiatric-outcome comparison, so no psychiatric edge is authored on that basis (negative-cohort and zero-record guards).

Negative screens recorded 2026-09-24: (i) no cardiac-arrhythmia edge - inappropriate sinus tachycardia is itself a sinus arrhythmia, so the edge would restate the identity (constitutive/umbrella guard); (ii) no cardiomyopathy or congestive-heart-failure edge - the largest condition-specific cohort found no cardiomyopathy and a stable ejection fraction, and only case reports document tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (negative-cohort guard); (iii) no depressive-disorder or anxiety-disorder edge - the only located psychiatric data are comorbidity prevalences in one cohort without a psychiatric-outcome analysis, and the direction is plausibly inverted because panic and anxiety disorders are listed among the causes of secondary sinus tachycardia that the diagnosis requires excluding (direction-inversion and zero-record guards); (iv) no syncope, presyncope, or falls edge - no syncope or falls identity exists and vasovagal-syncope owns the reflex mechanism (wrong-target and parallel-pathway guards); (v) no exercise-intolerance, dyspnoea, or fatigue edge - no such catalog identities exist (wrong-target guard); (vi) no pulmonary-embolism, hyperthyroidism, or anaemia edge - those are differential causes of secondary tachycardia listed as exclusions rather than consequences of the syndrome, so the direction would be inverted (direction-inversion guard); (vii) duplicate-scope note: this batch adds the first inappropriate-sinus-tachycardia-primary window to the registry.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Review-level descriptions of the inappropriate sinus tachycardia syndrome document dizziness among its reported symptoms: the Ahmed 2022 JACC review describes the condition as a clinical syndrome associated with distressing symptoms whose most common symptom is palpitations but which can be accompanied by a myriad of symptoms including anxiety, dizziness, presyncope, and syncope, and the Ruzieh 2018 review defines it as a resting sinus rate inexplicably above one hundred beats per minute associated with symptoms such as palpitations, dyspnoea, or dizziness in the absence of primary causes of tachycardia - a reproducible co-occurrence association rather than an individual causal nexus.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established: the located evidence is review-level symptom enumeration rather than condition-specific measurement of incident dizziness, dizziness is plausibly attributable to the shared autonomic abnormality or to concurrent conditions rather than to the heart rate itself, and the diagnosis of inappropriate sinus tachycardia is one of exclusion that requires ruling out medications and substances, panic attacks, pulmonary embolism, fever, hyperthyroidism, hypovolaemia, anaemia, and pain; an individual determination therefore requires heart-rate and rhythm documentation with dates, symptom characterization and chronology, and exclusion of the competing causes of dizziness listed on this edge.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized multifactorial route is described: inappropriate sinus tachycardia is characterized by a resting sinus rate above the normal range without a primary cause, and the JACC 2022 review records that its pathogenesis is not well understood and considered multifactorial with autonomic dysfunction as the central abnormality, so cerebral perfusion and vestibular-autonomic signalling can be affected both by the sustained rate and by the underlying autonomic imbalance, which is why dizziness appears among the syndrome's reported symptoms alongside palpitations, anxiety, presyncope, and syncope; the review-level nature of the evidence and the overlap between the symptom complex and the syndrome definition leave individual attribution hypothesized.
causalMechanism.secondaryVector: Anxiety and panic symptoms coexist with the syndrome and can themselves produce dizziness and further raise the heart rate, and the differential list for secondary sinus tachycardia (pulmonary embolism, anaemia, hypovolaemia, hyperthyroidism, fever, medications, and pain) contains several independent causes of dizziness, so the symptom may reflect either the syndrome or one of its mimics.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The edge asserts an association only: two review-level descriptions of the inappropriate sinus tachycardia syndrome list dizziness among its reported symptoms, but the evidence is symptom enumeration rather than condition-specific measurement of incident dizziness, the diagnosis is one of exclusion with a differential list that itself contains causes of dizziness, and the syndrome's mechanism is described as multifactorial with autonomic dysfunction rather than a demonstrated tachycardic mechanism, so no at-least-as-likely-as-not probability is asserted and an individual claim requires rhythm documentation with chronology, symptom characterization, and exclusion of competing causes.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Heart-rate and rhythm documentation (electrocardiogram with rate, Holter or event-monitor recordings, and the postural and exertional heart-rate behaviour) with dates; documentation of the diagnostic exclusion of secondary causes including thyroid function, haemoglobin, electrolytes, medication and substance review, and pulmonary embolism where relevant; characterization of the dizziness (episodic versus positional, duration, associated palpitations, presyncope, or syncope) with a symptom diary or orthostatic vital signs; chronologic relationship of the dizziness to the documented tachycardia; age and sex context, since the syndrome predominantly affects young women; assessment of competing causes including vestibular disorders, orthostatic and reflex syncope, anxiety or panic disorder, anaemia, dehydration, and medication effects; cardiology, neurology, or otolaryngology assessment of whether the documented tachycardia materially contributed to the dizziness
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Vestibular disorders (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular neuritis, or migraine-associated vertigo)
Orthostatic hypotension, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or reflex syncope
Anxiety or panic disorder with autonomic arousal
Secondary sinus tachycardia from anaemia, hyperthyroidism, hypovolaemia, fever, pulmonary embolism, pain, or medications and substances
Medication effects and other cardiac arrhythmias such as atrial tachycardia or atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia

suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: the JACC 2022 review of inappropriate sinus tachycardia states that the syndrome is associated with distressing symptoms and that dizziness appears among them alongside palpitations, anxiety, presyncope, and syncope, and the Ruzieh 2018 review defines the syndrome by an inexplicable resting sinus rate above one hundred beats per minute with symptoms such as palpitations, dyspnoea, or dizziness in the absence of primary causes, establishing a reproducible co-occurrence association; the edge is not raised to causation because the evidence is review-level symptom enumeration rather than condition-specific incident measurement, the mechanism is described as multifactorial with autonomic dysfunction, and the diagnosis is one of exclusion whose differential list contains independent causes of dizziness, so the consensus remains NOT_ESTABLISHED with rhythm documentation, exclusion, characterization, chronology, and competing-cause requirements and no probability estimate is asserted.
